It appears only twice in the Old Testament — once in Genesis 15:17, where it describes the cut animal pieces in Abraham's covenant ritual, and once in Psalm 136:13, where it refers to the divided parts of the Red Sea. The KJV translates it as both 'part' and 'piece,' which captures its narrow range well. Notably, the LXX renders it once as φλόξ ('flame') in the Psalm passage, suggesting ancient translators sometimes interpreted the context quite freely.

It appears 15 times across 5 books, concentrated especially in Joshua (5×), 1 Chronicles (4×), and 1 Kings (3×), reflecting its importance in conquest narratives, tribal boundaries, and Solomonic administrative records. The LXX translations are unusual — rendering the name twice as φόρος (tribute) and once as ἐκκεντέω (to pierce through) — suggesting ancient translators occasionally misread or reinterpreted the text rather than consistently treating it as a proper noun.

It appears 18 times across 7 books, with notable concentration in Psalms, 2 Samuel, and Proverbs, spanning both vivid poetic imagery (coals flying from God's nostrils in Ps/2 Sam) and practical ritual use (Leviticus 16 for the altar). The LXX translators overwhelmingly chose ἄνθραξ ("coal" or "carbuncle") 11 out of 18 times, confirming ancient readers understood this as hot, glowing charcoal rather than any broader fire term.
